subject: Archaeology
title: Satellite Archaeology from Space
description: Learn Satellite Archaeology from Space in one minute.

hook.text: Sarah Parcak uses satellite images to find buried pyramids and tombs from her laptop. She has found thousands of sites.

buildup.text: Infrared satellite imagery detects subtle differences in soil and vegetation that indicate buried structures below.

discovery.text: Parcak identified 17 potential pyramids, 3,100 settlements, and 1,000 tombs in Egypt alone using satellite data.

twist.text: Looting is also visible from space. Satellite images show pockmarked landscapes where robbers have dug illegal pits.

climax.text: Parcak launched GlobalXplorer, a platform where volunteers analyze satellite images to spot looting and hidden ruins.

punchline.text: You can hunt for pyramids from your couch.

quiz.question: What can satellite archaeology detect besides buried structures?
options: The age of buried artifacts using infrared dating
Evidence of looting — pockmarked landscapes from illegal digging
Underground water sources used by ancient civilizations

details.summary: Satellite archaeology uses multispectral imagery, radar, and thermal data from orbiting sensors to detect archaeological sites from space. Buried walls, ditches, and roads alter soil moisture, plant growth, and thermal properties in ways that satellites can detect across vast landscapes.
details.whyItMatters: Satellites survey entire countries in hours, identifying thousands of potential sites that would take ground teams decades to find. In politically unstable regions where ground access is impossible, satellite survey may be the only viable option.
takeaways: Multispectral satellites detect buried features through vegetation changes
Enables survey of vast areas inaccessible to ground teams
Sarah Parcak pioneered the field using declassified spy satellite data

faq.question: How can satellites detect buried archaeological features?
faq.answer: Buried walls restrict root growth and moisture, causing crops above them to ripen earlier or grow shorter. Satellites detect these subtle differences in near-infrared wavelengths. Radar can penetrate shallow soil in arid regions to reveal features directly beneath the surface.

faq.question: How has satellite archaeology been used to combat looting?
faq.answer: Comparing satellite images over time reveals new looting pits — dark dots appearing in previously undisturbed sites. Sarah Parcak's research documented thousands of new looting pits in Egypt after the 2011 revolution, providing evidence for heritage protection agencies.
